us2008-069: Washington led the Continental Army to victory in the Revolutionary War and became the first President in 1789. Because of his role in founding the nation, he is called the 'Father of Our Country.'
us2008-070: George Washington became the first President in 1789 and served two terms. He chose to step down after eight years, which started a two-term tradition.
us2008-071: In 1803, under President Jefferson, the U.S. paid France about $15 million for the Louisiana Territory, west of the Mississippi River. It doubled the size of the country.
us2008-072: The War of 1812 was against Britain, the Mexican-American War (1846-1848) against Mexico, and the Spanish-American War (1898) against Spain. The Civil War (1861-1865) was between the North and the South.
us2008-073: Eleven Southern states tried to leave the United States and formed the Confederacy. The war lasted from 1861 to 1865, and the North (the Union) won, keeping the country together.
us2008-074: The North and South disagreed about slavery, including whether it could spread to new western territories. The South's farm economy depended on enslaved labor, while the North had more factories.
us2008-075: Lincoln was President during the Civil War and worked to keep the country united. In 1863 he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which declared enslaved people in the Confederate states free.
us2008-076: President Lincoln issued it on January 1, 1863, during the Civil War, to free enslaved people in the Confederate states. The 13th Amendment ended slavery in the whole country in 1865.
us2008-077: Anthony spent decades working for women's right to vote and was arrested for voting in 1872. The 19th Amendment, which protects women's right to vote, was added in 1920, after her death.
us2008-078: The U.S. fought in both world wars, then in Korea and Vietnam during the Cold War. The Persian Gulf War, in 1991, forced Iraq's army out of Kuwait.
us2008-079: Woodrow Wilson was President from 1913 to 1921. He asked Congress to declare war on Germany in 1917, after German submarines attacked American ships.
us2008-080: Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR) was elected four times, more than any other president, and served from 1933 until his death in 1945. His New Deal programs were created to fight the Depression.
us2008-081: Japan, Germany, and Italy were called the Axis Powers. The U.S. entered the war after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941.
us2008-082: As a general in World War II, Eisenhower led the D-Day invasion of France on June 6, 1944. He later served as President from 1953 to 1961.
us2008-083: During the Cold War, the U.S. and the communist Soviet Union competed for power around the world. The U.S. worked to stop communism from spreading to other countries.
us2008-084: In the 1950s and 1960s, people used peaceful protests to fight segregation (separating people by race). Their work helped pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
us2008-085: King, a minister, led peaceful protests against racial discrimination. At the 1963 March on Washington, he gave his famous 'I Have a Dream' speech.
us2008-086: On September 11, 2001, terrorists took over four airplanes. They crashed two into the World Trade Center in New York City, one into the Pentagon, and one in a Pennsylvania field.
us2008-087: There are hundreds of American Indian tribes in the United States, each with its own history, culture, and government. The Cherokee and the Navajo are two of the largest.
us2008-088: The Mississippi flows from Minnesota south to Louisiana, and the Missouri River joins it near St. Louis. Together they form one of the largest river systems in the world.
us2008-089: The Pacific is the largest ocean in the world. California, Oregon, Washington, Alaska, and Hawaii all have Pacific coastlines.
us2008-090: The East Coast runs along the Atlantic Ocean from Maine to Florida. All 13 original colonies were in this eastern part of the country.
us2008-091: Territories belong to the United States but are not states. Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands are in the Caribbean, and Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands are in the Pacific.
us2008-092: The U.S.-Canada border is the longest border between two countries in the world. Thirteen states touch it, including Alaska and some states whose border runs through the Great Lakes.
us2008-093: Four states, from California in the west to Texas in the east, border Mexico. Part of the border follows the Rio Grande, the river between Texas and Mexico.
us2008-094: D.C. stands for District of Columbia, a federal district that is not part of any state. The city is named after George Washington and has been the capital since 1800.
us2008-095: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from the people of France, dedicated in 1886. It stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor and became a symbol of welcome for immigrants.
us2008-096: The 13 red and white stripes stand for the 13 colonies that declared independence in 1776. The stripes stay at 13, but a star is added for each new state.
us2008-097: Each of the 50 stars stands for one state. The 50-star flag has been used since 1960, after Hawaii became the 50th state in 1959.
us2008-098: Francis Scott Key wrote the words during the War of 1812, when he saw the flag still flying over Fort McHenry after a British attack in 1814. It became the national anthem in 1931.
us2008-099: On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. Americans celebrate the nation's birthday with parades, picnics, and fireworks.
us2008-100: These are federal holidays, when most federal offices close. Some fall on a fixed date, like Independence Day on July 4, while others fall on a set Monday, like Labor Day in September.
